newsitem.title: UK: S&P sees Central, Eastern Europe bond issues rising.
newsitem.headline: S&P sees Central, Eastern Europe bond issues rising.

text.p: Eurobond issuance out of the transition economies of Central and Eastern Europe is accelerating, with tighter spreads, longer maturities, and a wider variety of currencies and types of entities issuing, Standard & Poor's said on Monday.
Issuance from the region is expected to reach $15-20 billion this year (including private placements), compared with about $5.0 billion last year," S&P said in CreditWeek.

"This trend is showing greater acceptance of low investment grade as well as speculative grade credit risk since the Eurobond investor traditionally has been credit-risk averse," said George Dallas, S&P's managing director of Eastern Europe, Middle East and Africa.
Spreads are tight. Slovenia's seven-year 400 million mark deal in May was the tightest ever and some issues such as the City of Moscow and St. Petersburg are heavily over-subscribed.

Sovereign issuers have begun to move into currencies other than the dollar to broaden their investor base ahead of a European single currency and gain recognition with European investors. The mark is particularly popular with Poland, Russia, Romania, Slovenia, and Croatia all issuing in this currency.

"Russia and the Czech Republic have paved the way for municipal issuance, and muncipalities and regions from many of the other countries are preparing to issue Eurobonds," the article said. "The next stage will see a far greater number of public utilities and corporates issuing bonds."
It said a number of utilities had natural monopolies and strong business profiles which gave them the potential for high credit quality.
"Many potential issuers are being held back by lack of necessary legal and accounting systems and high withholding taxes," it said. "But countries are now addressing these problems."
